eventSummary.en: Early tradition (and Galatians 2:11) connects Peter with Antioch before his later association with Rome; he is counted as its first bishop in church tradition.

disputes.en: Peter's presence at Antioch is supported by Galatians 2:11, but the 'first bishop' tradition is later church tradition, not Scripture.

eventSummary.en: Strong and early tradition places Peter's later ministry and martyrdom at Rome under Nero. '1 Peter 5:13' greets from 'Babylon', widely read as a cryptonym for Rome. Acts does not narrate this.

disputes.en: Peter's Roman martyrdom is early and widely attested in tradition but not recorded in the New Testament; the 'Babylon=Rome' reading of 1 Peter 5:13 is the usual but not the only interpretation.

eventSummary.en: Tradition (Irenaeus, Eusebius) places the apostle John's later years at Ephesus, leading the churches of Asia.

disputes.en: The Ephesian residence of John rests on second-century tradition; the identity of 'John' of Revelation, the Gospel and the elder is itself debated.

eventSummary.en: Revelation 1:9 says its author was on Patmos 'for the word of God and the testimony of Jesus'; tradition reads this as exile under Domitian.

disputes.en: Patmos as a place of John's exile is stated in Revelation; the Domitianic dating and the exile interpretation are traditional.

eventSummary.en: Tradition places the apostle (or evangelist) Philip's ministry and martyrdom at Hierapolis; an octagonal martyrium has been excavated there.

disputes.en: Sources conflate Philip the apostle and Philip the evangelist (Acts) at Hierapolis; the martyrium confirms veneration, not the historical events.

eventSummary.en: Coptic tradition credits Mark the Evangelist with founding the church of Alexandria and being martyred there.

disputes.en: Mark's founding of the Alexandrian church is firm Coptic tradition but is not recorded in the New Testament.

eventSummary.en: Genesis opens Abraham's story at Ur, from which Terah's family set out for Canaan (Genesis 11:31).
The family settles at Haran; there Abraham receives the call to go to a land God will show him, with the promise of blessing (Genesis 12:1-4).
Entering Canaan, Abraham builds his first altar at the oak of Moreh near Shechem, where the land is promised to his offspring (Genesis 12:6-7).
Abraham pitches between Bethel and Ai and builds an altar (Genesis 12:8); Jacob later dreams here of the ladder to heaven (Genesis 28).
Abraham settles by the oaks of Mamre at Hebron and buys the cave of Machpelah to bury Sarah — the patriarchs' traditional tomb (Genesis 23).
At Beersheba Abraham and Isaac dig wells and swear covenants; it becomes the patriarchs' southern frontier (Genesis 21:31; 26:23-33).

display.en: c. 1446 BC (early date) or c. 1260 BC (late date) — debated

eventSummary.en: Israel departs Egypt from the region of Rameses in Goshen after the plagues and the first Passover (Exodus 12:37).

disputes.en: The Exodus route and its date (early c. 1446 BC vs late c. 1260 BC) are debated, and the wilderness stations cannot be securely mapped; the geography here follows the biblical itinerary, not confirmed archaeology.

display.en: c. 1446 BC (early date) or c. 1260 BC (late date) — debated

eventSummary.en: At the mountain of God (Sinai/Horeb) Israel receives the Law and enters the covenant (Exodus 19-20). The mountain's location is uncertain.

disputes.en: Both the Exodus date and the identity of Mount Sinai are disputed; the traditional Jebel Musa is used with alternatives noted on the site.

display.en: c. 1446 BC (early date) or c. 1260 BC (late date) — debated

eventSummary.en: From Kadesh-barnea Israel sends spies into Canaan and, after the refusal to enter, spends its wilderness years (Numbers 13; 20).

disputes.en: The Exodus route and its date (early c. 1446 BC vs late c. 1260 BC) are debated, and the wilderness stations cannot be securely mapped; the geography here follows the biblical itinerary, not confirmed archaeology.

display.en: c. 1446 BC (early date) or c. 1260 BC (late date) — debated

eventSummary.en: On Mount Nebo Moses views the promised land he will not enter, and dies (Deuteronomy 34).

disputes.en: The Exodus route and its date (early c. 1446 BC vs late c. 1260 BC) are debated, and the wilderness stations cannot be securely mapped; the geography here follows the biblical itinerary, not confirmed archaeology.

display.en: c. 1446 BC (early date) or c. 1260 BC (late date) — debated

eventSummary.en: Under Joshua, Israel crosses the Jordan near Jericho into Canaan (Joshua 3-6). The Late-Bronze destruction of Jericho and its dating are debated.

disputes.en: The archaeology of Jericho's fall (dating of the destruction at Tell es-Sultan) is much debated and does not cleanly fit either Exodus date.

eventSummary.en: Warned in a dream, Joseph took the child and his mother by night to Egypt to escape Herod's massacre of the infants of Bethlehem, and stayed until Herod's death — which Matthew reads as fulfilling 'Out of Egypt I called my son' (Hosea 11:1; Matthew 2:13-15). Only Matthew records the flight; the exact refuge is unknown, though Coptic tradition venerates a string of sites along the Nile (Old Cairo's Abu Serga, Wadi El Natrun, Asyut). The family then returned and settled in Nazareth (Matthew 2:19-23).

disputes.en: The flight into Egypt is attested only in Matthew and its route and Egyptian location are traditional; the mapped point (Old Cairo) is one of several Coptic-tradition sites, not an archaeologically fixed spot.

eventSummary.en: At Passover, when Jesus was twelve, the family made the pilgrimage to Jerusalem; on the way home his parents realised he was missing and, after three days, found him in the temple courts 'sitting among the teachers, both listening to them and asking them questions.' Asked why, he answered, 'Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house?' (Luke 2:41-49). It is the only canonical episode between the infancy and the baptism; Luke closes it noting he 'grew in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man' (Luke 2:52).

display.en: Scripture: 2348 BC (Ussher); flood silt at Shuruppak c. 2900 BC

eventSummary.en: Noah is commanded to build the ark — gopher wood, three decks, 300 cubits (~137 m) long (Genesis 6:14-16) — and enters it with his family and the animals as the fountains of the great deep break open (Genesis 7:11-12). Scripture does not name the building site; the Mesopotamian flood tradition centers on Shuruppak, whose excavated flood silt (c. 2900 BC) sits in the same window as Ussher's 2348 BC date and anchors the setting.

display.en: Scripture: 2348 BC (Ussher); flood silt at Shuruppak c. 2900 BC

eventSummary.en: 'And the ark rested in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, upon the mountains of Ararat' (Genesis 8:4). Noah releases the raven and the dove, leaves the ark, builds an altar (Genesis 8:18-20), and receives the rainbow covenant (Genesis 9:12-17). Candidates for the landing carry precise GPS points — Greater Ararat 39.7019° N 44.2983° E, Durupınar 39.4406° N 44.2347° E, Mount Cudi 37.3694° N 42.3442° E.

disputes.en: Genesis names the Urartu mountain region, not a peak. The Durupınar GPR scans (2019) and soil analyses (2022-2024) reported by the Noah's Ark Scans team are not peer-reviewed, and mainstream geologists identify the formation as a natural syncline; medieval-and-later tradition favors Greater Ararat, while the oldest traditions name Mount Cudi.

display.en: Scripture: 2348 BC (Ussher); flood silt at Shuruppak c. 2900 BC

eventSummary.en: After the Flood, Noah lives 350 more years (Genesis 9:28) and the table of nations spreads from his sons. Journeying from the east, the post-Flood generations find a plain in the land of Shinar and settle there, building the city and tower of Babel (Genesis 11:2-4) — returning the story to the Mesopotamian plain where it began.
Hannah brought the child to Eli at the house of the LORD in Shiloh, and there Samuel received the word that would end Eli's house.

Israel took the ark out of Shiloh into battle against the Philistines at Aphek and lost it, with Eli's sons killed and Eli dead at the news. Shiloh's burnt destruction layer belongs to about this generation.
Samuel gathered the nation at Mizpah to put away foreign gods, and the Philistine attack on the assembly broke; he set up the stone he named Ebenezer.

title.en: The circuit and the demand for a king

eventSummary.en: Samuel judged Israel year by year from Bethel to Gilgal to Mizpah and back to Ramah, where his house was — and where the elders came demanding a king like the nations.
After the relief of Jabesh-gilead the people renewed the kingdom at Gilgal and made Saul king before the LORD; Samuel gave his farewell address there.

disputes.en: Gilgal is unlocated — several tells near Jericho have been proposed and none confirmed.

eventSummary.en: Sent to Jesse's house with a horn of oil, Samuel passed over seven sons before the youngest was called in from the sheep and anointed in the midst of his brothers.
The youngest son of Jesse, keeping sheep, was anointed by Samuel while Saul still reigned.
The armies faced each other across the Elah valley between Socoh and Azekah, and the shepherd who had come with provisions for his brothers went out to the champion with a sling.

title.en: Saul's court, and flight from it

eventSummary.en: Brought into the king's household and given command, David's success turned Saul's favour to suspicion, and he escaped through a window by night.

title.en: The cave, and four hundred men

eventSummary.en: At the cave of Adullam in the Shephelah his family came down to him, and everyone in distress, in debt or discontented gathered to him — about four hundred men.
In a cave among the strongholds of En-gedi, with Saul within reach, David cut off the skirt of his robe and would not raise his hand against the anointed king.

title.en: Sixteen months as a Philistine vassal

eventSummary.en: Achish of Gath gave him Ziklag as a border holding; while he was away with the Philistine muster, Amalekite raiders burned the town and carried off the families, and he pursued and recovered them all.

disputes.en: Ziklag's location is contested — Khirbet a-Ra'i, Tell esh-Sharia and Tel Halif are all argued, and no inscription names the town.

eventSummary.en: After Saul's death on Gilboa, the men of Judah anointed David king at Hebron, where he reigned seven and a half years before the northern tribes came to him.
David took the Jebusite stronghold, made it the city of David, and brought the ark up into it — a capital belonging to neither Judah nor the northern tribes by inheritance.
Driven out of his own capital by his son's revolt, David crossed the Jordan to Mahanaim in Gilead, where the decisive battle was fought in the forest of Ephraim.
He appears without introduction before Ahab: 'As the LORD God of Israel liveth… there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word.'

disputes.en: Tishbe is unlocated; Listib in Gilead preserves the name, and one reading of the Hebrew removes the place name altogether.

eventSummary.en: Hidden by the brook Cherith before Jordan through the first of the drought years, until the brook itself dried up.

disputes.en: The wadi is unlocated. Wadi al-Yabis fits the description and lies below the traditional Tishbe, but the text names no more than 'before Jordan'.

eventSummary.en: Sent out of Israel entirely, to a Phoenician town belonging to Sidon — Jezebel's own country — where a widow's meal and oil did not fail and her son was restored to life.

title.en: Obadiah, and the meeting with Ahab

eventSummary.en: In the third year, sent back to show himself to Ahab. Obadiah, the king's steward hiding a hundred prophets in caves, brought word, and the king met him with 'Art thou he that troubleth Israel?'

title.en: The contest with the prophets of Baal

eventSummary.en: Four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal against one, an altar of twelve stones, water poured into the trench, and the fire that fell — then the slaughter at the brook Kishon.

disputes.en: The mountain is certain; the spot is not. El-Muhraqa has carried the tradition since the Middle Ages, but the text names no site.

title.en: Rain, and the run before the chariot

eventSummary.en: A cloud the size of a man's hand rose out of the sea, the drought broke, and Elijah ran before Ahab's chariot to the entrance of Jezreel — where Jezebel's message sent him running again.

title.en: A day's journey into the wilderness

eventSummary.en: He left his servant at Beersheba, went a day's journey into the wilderness, sat down under a juniper tree and asked to die; an angel fed him twice for the road ahead.
Forty days to the mount of God, and there the wind, the earthquake and the fire, and after them a still small voice — and the commission to anoint Hazael, Jehu and Elisha.

disputes.en: Horeb/Sinai's location is itself disputed; the traditional Jebel Musa is a Byzantine identification and several northern and Midianite candidates are argued.

eventSummary.en: He found Elisha ploughing with twelve yoke of oxen, threw his mantle over him in passing, and the young man burned his plough, boiled the oxen, and followed.

disputes.en: Abel-meholah is placed by rival candidates on either bank of the Jordan.

eventSummary.en: From Gilgal to Bethel to Jericho and over a parted Jordan, with Elisha refusing to be left behind — then the chariot of fire, and the mantle that fell.
Ploughing his father's land when Elijah's mantle fell on him; he asked leave to kiss his parents goodbye, then destroyed his own means of going back.

title.en: The mantle, and the spring healed

eventSummary.en: He took up the mantle that fell, parted the Jordan with it, and the prophets at Jericho said the spirit of Elijah rested on him; he healed the town's bad water with salt.
Going up from Jericho to Bethel — a royal sanctuary of the northern kingdom — he was mocked by a crowd of youths, and two she-bears came out of the wood.
Carmel, where Elijah's contest had been fought, became a place Elisha kept and where those in trouble knew to look for him.
A well-off woman built a small walled chamber on the roof for the prophet's circuit; the son promised to her died of sunstroke in the harvest field, and she rode to Carmel to fetch Elisha.
A famine year at the prophetic guild in Gilgal: wild gourds shredded into the stew, and meal thrown in to make it edible; then twenty barley loaves that fed a hundred with some left.

disputes.en: Gilgal is unlocated, and the Old Testament uses the name of more than one place.

eventSummary.en: The king of Aram sent a force by night to take the prophet whose warnings kept spoiling his raids; the servant saw the town surrounded, and the army that came for Elisha was struck blind and led into Samaria.
Samaria besieged and starving, with a donkey's head selling for eighty pieces of silver — and four lepers at the gate who found the Aramean camp abandoned overnight.

title.en: Hazael and the king of Aram

eventSummary.en: Ben-hadad sent Hazael to ask the Israelite prophet whether he would recover; Elisha wept as he told Hazael what he would do to Israel, and Hazael went home and took the throne.
Elisha sent one of the sons of the prophets with a box of oil to the army camp at Ramoth-gilead; the coup that followed ended the house of Omri, and Assyrian records date Jehu's tribute to 841 BC.
Sent to Nineveh, he went down to Joppa, found a ship going to Tarshish, paid the fare and went aboard 'from the presence of the LORD'.
The intended destination — in the Hebrew Bible the far west, the edge of the known world. The storm, the lots and the sailors' reluctant decision ended the voyage well short of it.

disputes.en: Tarshish is unidentified: Tartessos in south-west Spain, Tarsus in Cilicia and a Sardinian identification are all argued. Read the pin as a direction of travel, not a located port.

eventSummary.en: Three days and nights in the fish, a prayer from inside it, and a return to the Levantine coast — the text names no landing place, so the pin returns to the port he sailed from.

disputes.en: The place he was put ashore is not named. The stop is anchored back at Joppa for the map's sake, not because the text locates it there.

title.en: Forty days, and a city that repented

eventSummary.en: A day's walk into the great city with a five-word sermon, and from the king down the city turned — then Jonah sat east of it under a withering gourd, angry that it had.
A priest's son from the Benjaminite town three miles from Jerusalem: 'Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee.' His own townsmen later plotted against his life.

disputes.en: Anathoth is placed either at the village of Anata, which preserves the name, or at Ras el-Kharrubeh a kilometre south, which has the Iron Age remains.

title.en: The temple sermon, and the burned scroll

eventSummary.en: He stood in the gate of the LORD's house and told Judah that the temple was no charm — Shiloh had been a sanctuary too. The scroll Baruch wrote was cut up and burned column by column, and rewritten with more added; Jeremiah himself was let down into a cistern in the court of the guard.
Taken in chains with the deportees as far as Ramah, the staging point for the march to Babylon, and there singled out by Nebuzaradan and given the choice of going or staying.
He went to Gedaliah, the governor Babylon installed over the remnant at Mizpah — until Gedaliah was assassinated at a meal and the survivors panicked.

Against his explicit counsel the remnant fled to Egypt and took him with them. At Tahpanhes he hid stones in the clay pavement at the entry of Pharaoh's house, and said Nebuchadnezzar would set his throne on them.

First the young men of the royal seed in 605, then the king, the craftsmen and the smiths with Ezekiel in 597, and finally the city itself in 586 — walls broken down, the temple burned, and the vessels carried away.
Taken fleeing near Jericho, the last king of Judah was brought to Nebuchadnezzar's headquarters on the Orontes; his sons were killed in front of him, and that was the last thing he saw.

disputes.en: Ribleh on the Orontes preserves the name and suits every notice in Kings and Jeremiah, but the site is unexcavated.

eventSummary.en: Trained for three years in the language and learning of the Chaldeans, Daniel served through the reigns from Nebuchadnezzar to Cyrus — the interpreted dreams, the furnace, the writing on the wall, and the lions' den.

'As I was among the captives by the river of Chebar, the heavens were opened.' He sat seven days astonished among them at Tel-abib, and prophesied for twenty-two years — first that the city would fall, then, once word came that it had, of dry bones and a restored temple.

disputes.en: Tel-abib itself is unlocated. The Chebar is generally identified with the nāru kabaru canal in the Nippur region, where cuneiform archives from al-Yahudu record deported Judean families by name — so the pin marks the documented setting, not a located village.

eventSummary.en: 'I saw in a vision… I was at Shushan in the palace, which is in the province of Elam' — the ram and the he-goat, and the empires read off them.
In the first year of Cyrus, permission to go up and build — and about fifty thousand went, with the temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar had taken, under Zerubbabel and Jeshua the priest.

title.en: Foundation laid, and a temple finished

eventSummary.en: The foundation was laid to shouting and to the weeping of those old enough to remember the first house; the work then stalled for sixteen years until Haggai and Zechariah restarted it, and the temple was finished in the sixth year of Darius.

A priest and scribe 'ready in the law of Moses' came up with a royal commission, a second company, and silver and gold for the house — refusing an escort, because he had told the king that God's hand was on them.
Cupbearer to Artaxerxes in the citadel at Susa, he heard that the survivors were in distress and the wall broken down, and asked the king for timber and a commission.

A night ride around the ruined circuit, the work parcelled out family by family with a weapon in one hand, and the wall finished in fifty-two days — then Ezra reading the law aloud at the Water Gate from morning until midday.
The fisherman who had denied him stood up with the eleven and preached the first sermon of the church, quoting Joel on the Spirit poured out on all flesh.
When Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word, Peter and John were sent down — the first extension of the church past the boundary that mattered most.
On a circuit through the coastal plain he found a man eight years bedridden with palsy, and the towns of Lydda and Sharon turned to the Lord.

title.en: Tabitha, and the vision on the roof

eventSummary.en: Tabitha, the disciple full of good works, was raised in the upper room at Joppa; and on the roof of Simon the tanner's house by the sea Peter saw the sheet let down and was told to call nothing common.
A Roman centurion's household received the Spirit before they were baptized, and the argument about Gentiles was settled by an event rather than a ruling — 'Can any man forbid water?'
Arrested by Herod Agrippa I in the days of unleavened bread and released overnight; and at the council of Acts 15 he argued that Gentiles should not be burdened with the law.
Paul's own account: Peter ate with Gentile believers at Antioch until men came from James, then drew back — and was rebuked to his face for it.

1 Peter closes with greetings from 'the church that is at Babylon' — read since antiquity as Rome. Clement, Ignatius, Irenaeus and Eusebius attest a martyrdom there under Nero, and a first-century memorial under St Peter's marks where the tradition was already located by the mid-second century.

disputes.en: That Peter died at Rome is early, widespread and uncontradicted in the ancient sources, but it is tradition rather than documentation: no first-century text states it outright, and the identification of the bones found beneath the basilica is disputed.
